subject: astronomy
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Approximately how long is a sidereal day?
questions.explain: A sidereal day, one rotation of the Earth relative to the distant stars, lasts about 23 hours 56 minutes.

questions.q: What is the length of a mean solar day?
questions.explain: The mean solar day, the average interval between successive noon positions of the Sun, is defined as exactly 24 hours.

questions.q: Why is the sidereal day shorter than the solar day?
options: The Earth must rotate slightly more than 360 degrees for the Sun to return to the meridian because it has moved along its orbit
The Earth spins faster relative to the stars than relative to the Sun
The Moon slows the Earth's rotation during the day
The Sun physically moves closer to the Earth each day
questions.explain: During one rotation the Earth also advances along its orbit, so it needs a little extra turning to bring the Sun back to the meridian, making the solar day longer.

questions.q: A sidereal day is measured with respect to which reference?
questions.explain: Sidereal time is based on the Earth's rotation relative to the fixed background of distant stars.

questions.q: By roughly how much does the sidereal day differ from the solar day?
questions.explain: The sidereal day is about 4 minutes shorter than the mean solar day.

questions.q: A particular star crosses the meridian at 22:00 tonight. At approximately what time will it cross the meridian tomorrow night?
questions.explain: Because the sidereal day is about 4 minutes shorter, a given star crosses the meridian roughly 4 minutes earlier by clock time each successive night.

questions.q: Which instrument directly indicates apparent solar time?
options: A pendulum clock set to GMT
questions.explain: A sundial reads apparent solar time, determined by the actual position of the real Sun in the sky.

questions.q: The equation of time is the difference between which two quantities?
options: Apparent solar time and mean solar time
Local time and the time at Greenwich
questions.explain: The equation of time is defined as apparent solar time minus mean solar time.

questions.q: Which two effects together cause the equation of time?
options: The tilt (obliquity) of the Earth's axis and the eccentricity of the Earth's orbit
The Earth's rotation and the Moon's gravity
Atmospheric refraction and the Earth's magnetic field
questions.explain: The axial tilt and the elliptical, varying-speed orbit both cause the apparent Sun to run ahead of or behind the mean Sun through the year.

questions.q: At its largest positive value, by roughly how much is the apparent Sun ahead of the mean Sun, and when?
questions.explain: The equation of time reaches its greatest positive value of roughly +16 minutes in early November.

questions.q: What is the name of the figure-of-eight curve traced by the Sun's position when photographed at the same mean (clock) time throughout the year?
questions.explain: The analemma is the figure-of-eight path that arises from the combined effects of the equation of time and the Sun's changing declination.

questions.q: A sundial reads 12:00 and the equation of time is +10 minutes (apparent ahead of mean). What is the mean solar time?
questions.explain: Since apparent time minus mean time is +10 minutes, mean time is 12:00 minus 10 minutes, giving 11:50.

questions.q: Roughly how many times a year does a correctly aligned sundial agree with a clock keeping mean time (equation of time equal to zero)?
questions.explain: The equation of time passes through zero about four times a year, when apparent and mean solar time coincide.

questions.q: Who introduced the Julian calendar?
questions.explain: The Julian calendar was introduced by Julius Caesar in 45 BC, using a 365.25-day year with a leap day every four years.

questions.q: Who introduced the Gregorian calendar and in which year?
questions.explain: The Gregorian calendar was introduced by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582 to correct the drift of the Julian calendar.

questions.q: Under the Gregorian rule, a century year is a leap year only if it is divisible by which number?
questions.explain: Century years are leap years only when divisible by 400, so 2000 was a leap year but 1900 was not.

questions.q: Using the Gregorian rules, which of these years is a leap year?
questions.explain: 2000 is divisible by 400 so it is a leap year, whereas 1900, 2100 and 2200 are century years not divisible by 400.

questions.q: Why was the Gregorian reform of the calendar needed?
options: The Julian year of 365.25 days was slightly too long, so the calendar slowly drifted relative to the seasons
The Julian year had too few days, so the seasons occurred earlier each year
The Julian calendar ignored leap years entirely
The Julian calendar was based on the Moon rather than the Sun
questions.explain: The Julian year exceeded the tropical year by about 11 minutes, accumulating roughly 10 days of drift by 1582.

questions.q: Approximately how long is the tropical year?
questions.explain: The tropical year, the basis of the calendar and the cycle of the seasons, is about 365.2422 days long.

questions.q: When Britain adopted the Gregorian calendar in 1752, how many calendar days had to be removed to correct the accumulated error?
questions.explain: In 1752 Britain dropped 11 days, so 2 September was immediately followed by 14 September.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Astronomy (1AS0) specification; Time & the Calendar
